newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian cocaine king hit with more prison time.
newsitem.headline: Colombian cocaine king hit with more prison time.

text.p: Miguel Rodriguez Orejuela, the jailed leader of Colombia's notorious Cali drug mob, will be an old man before he walks free after having his sentence extended, judicial officials said on Monday.
Rodriguez, a 53-year-old billionaire known as "El Senor" (The Man), received a light prison term on Jan. 17 that would have allowed him to leave Bogota's La Picota prison in as little as five years.

But a "faceless" or anonymous judge in Bogota sentenced him to 23 years over the weekend and his final sentence, which will be dictated in the coming weeks, may be as high as 30 years, judicial officials told Reuters.
"Even with time off for good behaviour, it now looks certain that Miguel will be well into his 70s before he's free again," said one of the officials, who spoke on condition he not be identified.

Rodriguez's original sentence, which prompted an outcry in Washington, was handed down by an anonymous judge in Cali. It was based on crimes he had confessed to and was lighter than many judicial officials had expected because his lawyers managed to win the maximum benefits available under Colombia's elaborate plea-bargaining system.

The sentence handed down on Saturday is subject to no such benefits since it involves a crime -- the shipment of 330 pounds (150 kg) of drugs to Tampa, Florida, in 1989 -- that Rodriguez never confessed to.

Colombia has special tribunals of faceless judges as a security measure to protect them against assassination or intimidation by criminal drug gangs. The judge who handed down Saturday's sentence failed to maintain his anonymity, however, since he was offered a $1 million bribe on Rodriguez's behalf.
An arrest order was issued last week for a former Bogota judge who served as a go-between in offering the bribe, the prosecutor-general's office said in a statement.

Because of the attempted bribe and other "aggravating factors," Rodriguez could get a maximum 30 years in prison when his definitive sentence is handed down next month, sources close to Prosecutor-General Alfonso Valdivieso said.

Colombia's Congress approved a stiff increase in penalties for drug trafficking last week, increasing the maximum sentence from 24 to 60 years. But the law cannot be applied retroactively and will affect only crimes committed after it was signed into law on Friday by President Ernesto Samper.

Miguel Rodriguez and his older brother Gilberto are self-confessed leaders of the Cali drug cartel, the same mob that allegedly helped finance Samper's 1994 election campaign and once controlled up to 80 percent of the world's cocaine trade. Gilberto's five-year sentence is being appealed by the government and may also be increased substantially.
